title: Uncle Dewey Schmid and the blues left hand
summary: After moving to Lakeview, his vaudeville uncle Dewey Schmid (Wilbur Leroy) shows him a low-down blues left hand, to his mother's displeasure.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: Yes, he was a very good friend of the families. And his name was Edward Bordeaux, which was a French name, and I think the name was B-O-R-D-E-A-U-X. When did you first start playing professionally? Well, now there's a little gap in between, Charlie, that when I hit around ten years old, well, I actually took about a year, I guess, of private lessons. And then when I hit this period of about ten and a half to eleven years old, I kind of got disinterested. And we moved away from the Bank Street area out into Lakeview. And this brought me into close contact with an uncle of mine by the name of Dewey Schmid, who used to be an old vaudeville entertainer. Dewey Schmid. Dewey Schmid. But his stage name was Wilbur Leroy, L-E-R-O-Y. And he was quite a character who really, really loved good blues, you know, and he faked piano a little bit, you know. And every chance he'd get, he'd come around and he'd start showing me how to fake the left hand, you know. He'd say, why don't you do it this way, Omin, instead of doing it the way you're doing it right now, you know. And my mother would hear me playing this left hand the way he was telling me how to do it, you know. She'd come running and, you know, telling me, don't play like that, don't play like that. As soon as she'd go out and get out of the way, I'd start playing it again.
Was that more or less a ragtime bass you were using there, or was it?

Well, I wouldn't exactly say that it was a ragtime bass because it was sort of a real low-down, I'd say more of a blues honky-tonk style of bass that he used. It was something that the piano players used to use a lot, you know. They used that one, two, three, four, boom, you know. They'd get that sort of little one, two, three, one, two, three, four, one, you know, and then they'd sort of get that little skip beat in between, which was really a real good beat. In fact, I wouldn't classify it as a real ragtime beat. I think it was more of a jazz beat.
Well, now, is this how you kind of eased in professionally? Well, yes, I would. Right.
